results.input: UKCA CE machinery, electrical, EMC, radio equipment and technical file requirements for an outdoor mechatronic product

output.cautions: This is regulatory research, not a conformity assessment, certification, legal opinion, or substitute for a competent machinery/EMC/radio engineer and, where required, an Approved or Notified Body. Voltage alone does not determine the complete compliance route. Classification depends on the delivered product, included power supplies and batteries, moving mechanisms, radio functions, installation/use environment, and destination market. Standards are technical evidence rather than legislation and should be selected from the current official/designated or harmonised lists; verify their editions, transition dates, deviations, and any product-specific rules immediately before design freeze and market placement. The 2026 GB recognition and marking position is change-sensitive, so re-check the relevant GOV.UK sector page and legislation at each release.
output.findings:
For Great Britain (England, Scotland and Wales), the product should first be classified by function and configuration, then assessed against every applicable product regime; multiple regimes may apply cumulatively. The central official GB guidance says manufacturers must design to the applicable essential requirements, complete conformity assessment, compile and retain technical documentation and a Declaration of Conformity, apply the correct marking, provide identification and instructions, and maintain production conformity. The current GB framework recognises CE routes for many regulated products alongside UKCA under the Product Safety and Metrology (Amendment) Regulations 2024; the exact recognition route and any sector-specific conditions must be checked at release date. Northern Ireland is a separate route under the Windsor Framework: CE applies, and CE+UKNI is relevant where a UK Approved Body is involved. [1]

The Supply of Machinery (Safety) Regulations 2008 apply if the cassette is an assembly of linked parts, at least one moving, with a drive system, joined for a specific application; the definition also covers assemblies intended to be installed in a building or structure, assemblies of machinery, and partly completed machinery. A fan, pump, damper, louvre, actuator, or similar driven mechanism can therefore make machinery classification plausible, but the final determination depends on the product’s actual function and supply configuration. Before supply or putting into service in GB, the responsible person must satisfy the essential health and safety requirements, compile the technical file, provide safe-use information, perform the relevant conformity route, issue the appropriate UK or EU declaration, and affix the relevant marking. Machinery risk assessment should explicitly address moving parts, guarding, unexpected start, maintenance access, hot/cold surfaces, water ingress, condensate, outdoor installation, foreseeable misuse, control-system failures, and integration hazards. [2]

The Electrical Equipment (Safety) Regulations 2016 (GB LVD-equivalent) cover equipment designed for 50–1,000 V AC or 75–1,500 V DC. A nominal 24/48 V DC cassette is below the stated voltage scope, so the complete low-voltage product will generally not be within this regulation solely because it is electrical equipment. This is not a general safety exemption: machinery, EMC, radio, product-specific rules, battery-related rules, fire requirements, and general product/work-equipment duties may still apply; internal components operating at higher voltages or an included mains power supply may trigger separate obligations for those products. [3]

The EMC Regulations 2016 apply broadly to electrical/electronic apparatus liable to generate electromagnetic disturbance, subject to listed exclusions. Essential requirements are that generated disturbance stays below a level that prevents radio/telecommunications or other equipment from operating as intended, and that immunity is adequate for the intended environment. The manufacturer must prepare technical documentation, carry out the relevant conformity procedure, issue a DoC, mark the apparatus, retain documentation and the DoC for 10 years, label manufacturer/traceability details, supply clear English instructions, and control changes in design and referenced standards. For this outdoor cassette, the engineering compliance plan should cover DC/DC converters, PWM motor drives, fans/pumps, switching relays, long outdoor cables, sensor wiring, enclosure bonding/grounding strategy, transient and surge exposure, conducted and radiated emissions, electrostatic discharge, radiated/conducted immunity, fast transients, surge, voltage dips where relevant, and functional performance criteria during disturbances. [4]

If the cassette contains Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, LoRa, Zigbee, or another intentional transmitter/receiver, the Radio Equipment Regulations 2017 are potentially applicable instead of or in addition to the ordinary EMC route for the radio equipment. They address health and safety, EMC, and efficient use of the radio spectrum. Manufacturers must meet the essential requirements, ensure operation does not infringe applicable spectrum-use requirements, compile technical documentation, use the applicable conformity procedure, issue a UK or EU DoC, apply marking, retain technical documentation and the DoC for 10 years, provide English instructions and safety information, state restrictions or authorisation requirements, and maintain production conformity. Radio modules are not automatically transferable as a compliance shortcut: the host product, antenna arrangement, enclosure, power supply, software/firmware, duty cycle, and intended environment can affect the final assessment. [5]

The technical file should be treated as a controlled product record, not merely a test report folder. It should identify the product and variants, intended use and foreseeable misuse, design drawings and schematics, bills of materials and critical components, software/firmware versioning and safety-related control logic, risk assessment, applied standards/specifications and rationale, calculations, verification/validation evidence, EMC and radio test reports where applicable, environmental/IP and mechanical evidence, user and installation instructions, labels/markings, declarations, manufacturing controls, and change history. The file must be sufficiently complete for the manufacturer to demonstrate compliance and must be retained for the period specified by the applicable regime; the official EMC, electrical, and radio guidance expressly states 10 years, while the machinery guidance requires the technical file to be compiled and made available on request. [1] [2] [4] [5]

For CE sales into the EU/EEA, the project must separately check the EU Machinery Directive 2006/42/EC or the Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 timetable and applicability, the EMC Directive 2014/30/EU, the Radio Equipment Directive 2014/53/EU where radio is present, and any other applicable EU legislation. A UKCA assessment or UK Approved Body is not an EU CE conformity assessment basis. Conversely, a CE route may be recognised for GB only where the current GB sector guidance and legislation permit it. Use the official text and current market guidance at the point of placing on each market. [1] [2] [4] [5]
output.topic: UKCA/CE compliance framework for an outdoor 24/48 V DC mechatronic cassette

results.input: Innovate UK Smart Grants application criteria and current grant proposal expectations

output.cautions: The paused-programme status and the 2024 project-size rules are not a current open-call entitlement; they are the latest official guidance and published competition terms located, and a future replacement or pilot may change eligibility, dates, budget, funding rates, question wording and assessment criteria. Smart Grants guidance is funding guidance, not product, electrical, EMC, radio, machinery, environmental, building, battery, cybersecurity or market-access compliance certification. A SELV or nominal 24/48V design should not be presented as automatically safe or legally compliant; applicable standards, risk assessments, testing and conformity obligations must be assessed separately. Do not count grant award, eligibility, or assessor expectations as evidence that the cassette meets any technical or regulatory requirement.
output.findings:
As of 17 August 2026, Innovate UK states that Smart Grants were paused from January 2025 while tailored support was developed; applicants must therefore verify that a live Smart opportunity exists on the Innovation Funding Service before preparing a submission. The last concrete published rounds located were April and July 2024, both now closed. The standing Smart guidance describes the programme as supporting original, high-impact, commercially viable innovations in any industry or technology area, with a clear and sizeable market need, a robust plan for rapid commercialisation, and substantial UK economic benefit through growth, jobs, market expansion and/or exports. [1] [2]

The latest published July 2024 brief required all project work to be performed in the UK and the results to be exploited from or in the UK. A UK-registered SME had to lead or be a grant-claiming partner. Projects of 6–18 months had eligible costs of £100,000–£500,000 and could be single or collaborative; projects of 19–24 months had eligible costs of £100,000–£1 million and had to be collaborative. The 24V/48V nominal DC architecture is not itself a Smart-Grant eligibility category or technical exemption: the proposal must frame the cassette as genuinely new and ahead of comparable market offerings, not merely as routine product improvement. [2]

For the Hybrid SELV Micro-Climate Cassette, a credible application should define the unresolved technical and user need in outdoor micro-climate control; quantify the baseline and target performance; explain why the hybrid architecture, low-voltage power/control approach, environmental robustness and integrated sensing/firmware are novel; and identify the technical uncertainties requiring R&D. Innovate UK’s general R&D guidance distinguishes industrial research from experimental development: prototype build, demonstration, piloting, testing and validation in representative real-life conditions can qualify as experimental development, whereas routine or periodic changes to an existing product or production process do not. [3]

The proposal should be business-led and evidence a deliverable, realistic and adequately resourced route to return on investment, growth and market share after the project. It should connect work packages and milestones to measurable technical outcomes, validation environments, customer adoption, intellectual-property strategy, manufacturing scale-up, route to market, exploitation responsibilities, UK economic impact and export potential. The standing assessment guidance specifically looks for the identified need, why grant support is important, evidence of a market that will buy and use the result, and how the applicant will access and exploit that market; the full assessor matrix is competition-specific. Applications are assessed by three independent assessors, and the final funding decision remains with Innovate UK. [1]

Applications must be made through the Innovation Funding Service. For a collaborative bid, the lead and at least one other organisation must request grant funding, the collaboration and division of work must be justified, and no single organisation may claim more than 70% of total project costs. UK subcontractors are permitted where justified, appropriately procured and proportionate. Innovate UK performs eligibility and financial-viability checks, applies the UK subsidy-control framework, and requires eligible costs and evidence supporting claims. Labour claims are based on actual eligible costs and require timesheets/project records; the cost guidance also provides specific limits and records requirements for non-PAYE micro-companies, sole traders and partnerships. [2] [4] [5]
output.topic: Innovate UK Smart Grants — current status and proposal requirements

results.input: OpenFOAM k-epsilon and SST k-omega setup conventions for an annular plenum diffuser CFD case

output.cautions: These sources document OpenFOAM model behavior and software conventions, not product performance, safety, UKCA/CE conformity, EMC, low-voltage, machinery, building, grant, or other regulatory certification. Neither k-epsilon nor SST k-omega should be treated as universally accurate for an annular diffuser: diffuser separation, perforated-sheet jets, fan swirl, buoyancy, roughness, leakage, and transient operation can dominate results. Validate against measured flow rate, pressure drop, outlet velocity/temperature uniformity, and—where relevant—acoustic data; perform mesh, timestep/steady-convergence, turbulence-inlet, and model sensitivity studies. Confirm dictionary syntax against the exact OpenFOAM distribution and release used, since OpenCFD and OpenFOAM Foundation releases differ in file names and keywords.
output.findings:
OpenFOAM configures Reynolds-averaged turbulence through the `constant/momentumTransport` file in current releases, with `simulationType RAS`, `model kEpsilon` or `model kOmegaSST`, and `turbulence on`; older OpenCFD documentation uses the analogous `constant/turbulenceProperties` dictionary with `RASModel`. The official v13 guide lists both models for incompressible and compressible flows and states that model-specific coefficient dictionaries are optional, with defaults available and printable at startup. [1] [2]

For standard k-epsilon, OpenFOAM solves transport equations for turbulent kinetic energy `k` and dissipation `epsilon`. Its documented isotropic inlet estimates are `k = 3/2 (I Uref)^2` and `epsilon = Cmu^0.75 k^1.5/L`, where `I` is turbulence intensity and `L` a reference length. The model is widely used but can over-predict turbulent kinetic energy at stagnation points and requires near-wall treatment. The documented inlet choices include fixed value or `turbulentMixingLengthDissipationRateInlet`; wall choices include `kLowReWallFunction`, `kqRWallFunction`, and `epsilonWallFunction`. [3]

For SST k-omega, OpenFOAM documents a two-equation `k`/`omega` model intended to reduce the standard k-omega model’s free-stream sensitivity and capture flow separation. Its isotropic initialization is `k = 3/2 (I Uref)^2` and `omega = sqrt(k)/(Cmu^0.25 L)`. The documented inlet options include fixed value or `turbulentMixingLengthFrequencyInlet`, with constrained outlet and wall-function support. SST is therefore a sensible primary screening model for an annular plenum and diffuser where adverse pressure gradients, jet interaction, recirculation, or separation may control uniformity; standard k-epsilon is useful as a comparison case and often as a robust baseline for fully developed internal flow. [4]

For the cassette case, define the annular plenum, diffuser perforations/louvres, casing, fan or blower representation, and downstream room/outdoor domain explicitly. Use a mass-flow or velocity inlet at the fan/plenum entry only when the upstream device performance is known; otherwise represent the fan with a measured pressure-rise/flow curve or an appropriately validated momentum source. Use pressure-type outlets with adequate downstream extent, and report mass imbalance. Prescribe inlet `I` and `L` from measurements or a defensible upstream hydraulic scale rather than arbitrary defaults; for an annular passage, a first geometric scale may be hydraulic diameter, but sensitivity to `I`, `L`, and inlet profile should be demonstrated.

Mesh and wall treatment must be selected as a coupled decision. OpenFOAM’s guide requires compatible turbulence-field wall conditions: `epsilonWallFunction` for epsilon, `omegaWallFunction` for omega, `kqRWallFunction` or the relevant low-Re condition for k, and a matching `nut` wall function. A wall-function mesh should target the wall-function regime consistently across the cassette surfaces; a wall-resolved SST mesh should instead resolve the viscous sublayer with an appropriate near-wall treatment. Do not mix a nominal y-plus target, wall function, and discretization scheme without checking the actual y-plus distribution, separation locations, and grid convergence. [2] [5]

Because the project is nominally 24/48 V DC, that voltage class does not change the fluid turbulence equations. It may affect fan speed, heat generation, actuator operating points, and therefore boundary conditions or conjugate/ buoyant thermal models. The standard k-epsilon page explicitly notes that buoyancy contributions are not included; if natural-convection effects from electronics, solar loading, or heat exchangers matter, use a buoyant solver/model and verify the selected buoyancy-capable turbulence formulation rather than silently adding thermal effects to a non-buoyant setup. The UK origin likewise does not make an OpenFOAM model a UK compliance assessment. [3]
output.topic: OpenFOAM RANS setup for annular plenum diffuser

results.input: Web Bluetooth and Web Serial browser security, permissions and safety considerations for industrial diagnostic tools

output.cautions: These documents describe web-platform behavior, draft specifications, developer documentation, and general UK workplace electrical-safety guidance; they are not product approvals, conformity assessments, cybersecurity certifications, functional-safety evidence, EMC evidence, radio approval, or certification of SELV/LV equipment. Browser support, operating-system behavior, enterprise policies, Bluetooth profiles, USB drivers, permissions persistence, and draft-specification text can change, so verify the exact deployment browser version and test failure modes on the intended ruggedized hardware. UK obligations depend on the complete product, installation, workplace, supply chain, and intended use, including applicable electrical, EMC, radio, machinery, battery, environmental, and cybersecurity requirements; obtain competent UK engineering and regulatory review before field deployment.
output.findings:
Web Bluetooth and Web Serial are powerful, origin-scoped browser capabilities rather than unrestricted device drivers. Both require a secure context, normally HTTPS; both are experimental/limited-availability features, so a production diagnostic tool must define and test a supported browser/OS/device matrix rather than assume cross-browser availability [1] [4]. Web Bluetooth is restricted to Bluetooth Low Energy GATT peripherals, while Web Serial covers serial devices and USB or Bluetooth devices that expose a virtual serial port, such as USB CDC-ACM or Bluetooth SPP [1] [4].

A connection must be an explicit user-mediated event. Web Bluetooth requestDevice() requires transient user activation and an explicit permission grant; Web Serial requestPort() likewise requires user activation and a chooser. Previously granted devices/ports may be rediscovered, but the application should make the active device and permission state visible and provide a deliberate disconnect/revoke workflow [1] [2] [4] [5]. Permissions Policy is an additional gate: the default allowlist is self for both bluetooth and serial, and a cross-origin iframe requires explicit policy/header and iframe allowance. If policy blocks access, the user may not receive a prompt and the call can fail with a security error [1] [4] [6].

For Web Bluetooth, use narrow filters based on the cassette’s proprietary service UUID, manufacturer data, name prefix, or other stable identifying data; list only the required GATT services and optional services. After selection, the origin can access only services authorized in the request. The specification requires the browser to explain the capabilities represented by requested services, avoid class-wide pairing, allow users to inspect/revoke access, and blocklist vulnerable GATT services. However, characteristic and descriptor values remain arbitrary byte arrays, and the specification warns that unexpected values can attack device parsers; application-level validation, bounds checking, command allowlists, rate limits, authentication, replay protection, and firmware-side authorization remain necessary [2] [3].

For Web Serial, use vendor/product filters where possible; unfiltered requestPort() exposes every available device in the chooser. Custom Bluetooth RFCOMM service classes need to be explicitly allowed, and serial access can be lost through disconnects or fatal stream errors, so the tool must handle connect/disconnect events, framing, timeouts, cancellation, malformed input, and safe stream shutdown [4] [5]. Treat every received frame as untrusted input and every write as a potentially consequential control operation. Prefer a read-only commissioning/diagnostic mode by default, require a second deliberate confirmation for actuator, power, heater, fan, pump, valve, or firmware-update commands, and display target identity, measured bus voltage, command effect, and an emergency stop/service-isolation instruction before writes.

For a 24/48 V nominal DC cassette, SELV terminology does not remove the need for engineering controls: fault energy, battery capability, inductive loads, stored energy, reverse polarity, transients, wet/outdoor conditions, and inadvertent energisation must be assessed separately. HSE guidance says electrical equipment must be maintained to prevent danger and that work/testing should, wherever possible, be performed with the system dead; diagnostic software cannot substitute for isolation, competent-person procedures, protective hardware, fusing, current limiting, watchdogs, independent shutdown, or a safe firmware state [7] [8]. The browser API/security model is therefore an access-control layer, not evidence that the cassette, radio protocol, power electronics, firmware, or diagnostic workflow is safe or compliant.
output.topic: Web Bluetooth and Web Serial security for UK industrial DC diagnostics

results.input: automotive/industrial wiring harness segregation, connector selection and low-voltage DC protection practices

output.cautions: These sources are authoritative references or official guidance, not evidence that the Hybrid SELV Micro-Climate Cassette complies with any standard, regulation, grant condition or certification scheme. Exact requirements depend on whether the product is machinery, an electrical installation, a battery/PV system, radio equipment, or a vehicle-derived assembly; on GB versus Northern Ireland/EEA placement; and on the final source energy, environmental exposure, EMC profile and intended users. Obtain the licensed standards, perform electrical, thermal, mechanical, EMC, ingress and fault-current verification, and have the final design and conformity route reviewed by a competent UK engineer or conformity-assessment specialist.
output.findings:
For a UK-origin outdoor cassette, treat the 24/48 V system as a safety-critical low-voltage power-and-control assembly even though it may fall below the UK Electrical Equipment (Safety) Regulations 2016 voltage scope. The GB guidance states that those Regulations cover equipment from 50–1,000 V AC or 75–1,500 V DC; a nominal 24/48 V DC cassette is therefore generally outside that particular regime, but other product-safety, machinery, EMC, environmental and workplace duties can still apply. [1] The designer should document the applicable product legislation and standard set rather than infer exemption from voltage alone.

IEC 60204-1:2016+A1:2021 is the principal machinery-electrical reference when the cassette is machinery or forms part of a coordinated machine system. Its scope starts at the point where the supply connects to the machine electrical equipment, and the current consolidated edition specifically identifies clarified overcurrent protection, short-circuit current rating, protective bonding, control-circuit protection, EMC and technical-documentation requirements. [2] Use it as a design framework for protective bonding, isolation, control-circuit separation, fault-current withstand, marking and schematics; confirm the UK-adopted edition and any machine-specific Type-C or product standard.

Harness architecture should separate high-current DC feeders, switching/actuator wiring and sensitive sensor, communications or RF wiring by physical routing and functional segregation. Avoid long parallel runs between noisy power conductors and analogue, pulse, CAN/RS-485 or RF circuits; where crossing is unavoidable, cross at approximately 90 degrees, keep return conductors paired with their supply conductors to minimise loop area, and use twisted/shielded cable where the interface specification calls for it. Bond shields and chassis at a defined point or according to the applicable interface/EMC standard, avoiding accidental multi-point ground paths. IEC 60204-1’s revised EMC and control-circuit provisions support this approach, but it does not provide a universal spacing number for every cassette layout; spacing, shielding and filtering must be verified by EMC risk assessment and test.

ISO 19642-1 is a road-vehicle automotive-cable vocabulary and design-guideline document, and the series addresses cables used in road vehicles. [3] It can be a useful engineering reference for compact, vibration-resistant harness construction, conductor identification, terminal/crimp practices and cable performance, but it is not automatically the correct compliance standard for a fixed outdoor product. Select cable insulation, temperature, UV, oil/chemical resistance, flex life, abrasion resistance, conductor cross-section and voltage rating from the actual environment and current/voltage-drop calculations. Automotive connectors should only be selected where their rated current, voltage, temperature, mating cycles, vibration, sealing, locking/CPA features and terminal system are demonstrated for the cassette duty; an IP rating alone does not establish electrical or mechanical suitability.

Outdoor connector and enclosure selection should use IEC 60529 IP testing as an explicit requirement. The IEC explains that the IP code rates protection against solids and liquids, that the first numeral addresses solids/dust and the second liquids, and that the standard also includes access-to-hazardous-parts considerations and defined tests. [4] Specify the required IP level for the complete installed interface, including cable glands, backshells, seals, plugs, unused cavities, drainage/condensation control and mating state. Do not describe an enclosure as “waterproof” solely from a component datasheet, and do not assume a connector’s nominal IP rating survives repeated unmating, cable flexing, dirt, UV ageing or incorrect assembly.

Protection must be designed from the source fault energy, not merely the nominal voltage. HSE states that fuses and circuit-breakers must be correctly rated for the circuit they protect, and that cables, plugs, sockets and fittings must be robust and adequately protected for the working environment; it also recommends considering RCD protection for outdoor or wet work where an AC supply is involved. [5] For each battery, DC/DC converter, PV input and branch load, place appropriately rated DC overcurrent protection close to the energy source, select interrupt rating for the prospective short-circuit current, verify DC arc-extinguishing capability and polarity, and coordinate upstream/downstream devices so a branch fault does not unnecessarily remove the whole system. Size conductors and protection together using continuous current, inrush, ambient temperature, bundling derating, installation method, voltage drop and fault-clearing time. Provide a load-break isolator or service disconnect, clearly identify polarity and isolation points, and protect exposed conductors against abrasion, chafe, crush and inadvertent shorting.

National Grid’s 2024 NSI 12 guidance is a useful high-consequence LV-work benchmark, not a product standard. It defines dangerous potential in its own safety-rule context as over 55 V DC, recognises battery systems with currents that are not inherently limited as dangerous energy, requires preference for dead working, controlled isolation, proving dead, competent persons and fuse/equivalent protection on test instruments and leads, and stresses screening of adjacent live equipment. [6] A 24/48 V cassette may therefore still present serious arc, burn, fire and battery-energy hazards despite being below many statutory “low-voltage equipment” thresholds. Incorporate touch-safe barriers, finger-safe terminals, precharge/inrush control where capacitive loads exist, current-limited service/test points, labelled isolation, lockout provisions and a documented safe-working procedure.
output.topic: 24/48 V DC hybrid cassette wiring, connectors and protection
